title: Why Catholics ask Mary
hookLine: asking Mary to pray for us, as we ask friends to, not worshiping her (CCC 971)

lines: WHY DO CATHOLICS PRAY TO MARY?
cards: You text a friend: big interview tomorrow, pray for me? Or: my mom's surgery is at nine, keep her in your thoughts. People ask this across many faiths, and people with no faith ask a version of it too.
Nobody thinks you're worshiping your friend. You're asking someone who loves you to stand with you. Now a question Catholics get asked a lot, sometimes kindly, sometimes not: why do you pray to Mary?
Isn't that worship? Isn't God enough? It's a fair question, and Catholics have a clear answer.

teach.b: Intercession: going to someone on another's behalf. In the New Testament, believers ask each other for prayer again and again. The Letter of James says, in the Douay-Rheims: "pray one for another."
The First Letter to Timothy urges intercessions for all people. Catholics believe death doesn't end the family.
The saints in heaven are still part of the Church, still alive in God, and they can still pray for us; the Creed calls it the communion of saints.
So for Catholics, asking Mary is asking the person they see as closest to Jesus to do what friends do. And the Church draws a hard line here.
The Catechism says devotion to Mary is essentially different from the worship given to God alone.
In Catholic teaching Mary is honored above all the saints, but honored, not adored. And she isn't a second savior.

The same letter to Timothy says: "For there is one God, and one mediator of God and men, the man Christ Jesus." Catholics agree completely, and they say everything Mary does, she does through her son and pointing to him.
She notices the problem and tells Jesus, they have no wine.

teach.h: WHATSOEVER HE SHALL SAY TO YOU, DO YE.
teach.b: Then she tells the servants: "Whatsoever he shall say to you, do ye." That's Catholic intercession in two lines: she brings the need to him, and sends people to him. Christians hold this differently.
Orthodox Christians ask Mary's prayers too. Protestant churches generally teach praying to God directly and asking the living for their prayers.
That's the Mary week: Hannah, the name behind Anne, and Joachim, the Immaculate Conception, Theotokos, the seven sorrows, the Assumption, Guadalupe, and intercession.

how: Catholics ask Mary and the saints to pray for them, most often in the Hail Mary's 'pray for us sinners', in litanies that answer each title with 'pray for us', and on saints' feast days.

o: asking someone to pray to God on your behalf
a short pause between two parts of the Mass
worshiping Mary and the saints in place of God

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.

s: the Catechism says devotion to Mary is essentially different from the worship given to God alone.
asking for prayers is in the Bible
Catholics say Mary is a second savior
they say there's one mediator, Christ, and Mary always points to him.

games.q: you're Mary at the wedding at Cana. the wine has run out and the hosts will be embarrassed. what do you do?
o: tell Jesus, then tell the servants to do whatever he says.
games.why: she brings the need to him, then says: "whatsoever he shall say to you, do ye." Catholics see all intercession in those two moves.

practice: Think of one thing you're carrying that you haven't asked anyone to help carry, and one friend you trust, and picture asking them: would you pray for me, or keep me in your thoughts?
Notice if it's hard to ask, then turn it around: who might want you to pray for them? If you pray, you can hold them before God now.

wordCard.voice: Intercession. Stepping in on someone else's behalf: asking friends, and for Catholics the saints and Mary, to pray for us. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: pray for us. the answer to each title of Mary in the old litanies.

carryVoice: Your line: pray for us. One mediator, Christ, and many who pray with us. Day eighty-four.
